title: The Elephant Gambit: traps, model games and when to play it
outcomes: Names three traps of the Elephant Gambit (the bishop check on b5, the knight attacking the queen, the knight sacrifice on f7) and the count that refutes each, and one trap for Black
Distinguishes a trap from the book from a trap that happens in games, using sample sizes from our archive
Reads two real games move by move, finds the decisive errors for each side, and explains how the e-file and the king's place decided both
Reads archive numbers with a stated sample and says why a few specialists can skew them
Designs a small experiment to decide whether to play the gambit, with a hypothesis, a record and a sample size

steps.text: **What makes a trap work.** A trap needs a natural move with a forcing refutation: a double attack by pawns, a loose piece, a sacrifice with too little behind it. [I] In all four examples above the cure is the same: before you answer a move, count what is attacked and what defends it. Trap 3 catches the player who sacrifices (White); the others catch the side that makes the natural move.

steps.caption: What our archive shows. [S] Our TWIC and Lichess broadcast files hold 2,852 Elephant Gambit games; 2,842 replay legally and 1,101 reach this position, most from 2020 to 2026 and many from online titled events (so they favour fast, online play). White's fourth move: queen to e2 in 858 games (White scored 52%), knight to d4 in 118 (34%), knight to e5 in 82 (46%), knight to g1 in 30 (40%), bishop check in 11 (50%). Overall White scored 49%.

steps.text: **Reading the numbers.** [S] In the 1,101 games one Black player appears 93 times and White scored 64% against him; another appears 54 times and White scored 30%. Specialists can pull a figure in either direction, so the numbers describe the specialists as much as the move. [I] A fair test needs many different players, similar ratings and a stated sample.

**A real game.** Deac (rated 2625) against Gadimbayli (2470), Titled Arena, 3 April 2021, as recorded in the TWIC files [S]; Black won in 26 moves. We follow the first 20 moves, replayed move by move and checked by the engine at the decisive points. The question to carry: where does White's king get into trouble?

steps.text: **What the two games share.** In both, the e-file and the king's position decided the game. [I] In the first game White's king left e1 for d1 and never found shelter; in the second White blocked with the bishop and castled, and Black's attack ran out of pieces. The pin on the e-file is a fight for the king, not only for a pawn.

steps.caption: Black to move after 2.Nf3, the crossroads. [S] In the Lichess sample the usual 2...Nc6 was played in 498,025 games and White scored 53%; 2...d5 was played in 18,003 and White scored 50%. [V] The engine puts 2...d5 about half a pawn worse for Black than 2...Nc6 (White about +0.9 against +0.3). A gambit is a cost with a purpose.

steps.prompt: [H] Treat the gambit as an experiment. State your hypothesis (for example: against players of my level, 2...d5 scores at least as well as 2...Nc6), what you will record in each game, and how many games you will play before you decide.

fields.label: Number of games before I decide:

steps.text: **How big a sample?** [V] The score of a player over 20 games has a margin of error of about plus or minus 11 percentage points (one standard error, the square root of 0.25 over 20). Over 100 games it is about 5. [I] So ten games of your own tell you almost nothing. The Lichess samples are large, so three points there is not noise; but the players who choose 2...d5 are not the same players who choose 2...Nc6, so it still does not prove the move is better.

**When to play it.** The honest case for the Elephant Gambit is practical: opponents who know the queen move and the pin will keep an edge, and most players will not. [H] It suits fast games, a player who likes initiative, and a learner who wants to study king safety by doing; it suits badly someone who wants a sound repertoire for the long term. Decide by your own results, not by anyone's boast.

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in a few sentences, explain to a beginner one trap for White and one for Black, what a real game from this lesson showed about the e-file, and when you would play the gambit. Self-check afterwards: did you say when the trap works and when it fails, give an example a beginner could set up on a board, and name one mistake to avoid? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.

steps.text: **Recap.** 1. Traps need a natural move and a forcing reply: count what is attacked first. 2. The bishop check on move four runs into a pawn recapture that attacks two pieces. 3. Knight sacrifices on f7 fail when only the queen follows. 4. The e-file decides king safety for both sides. 5. A gambit costs roughly half a pawn against best play. 6. Archive numbers need a sample size and an eye on who played. 7. Run the experiment before you trust the story.
